label: Writing appears in Mesopotamia and Egypt
summary: Clay tablets from Uruk with numbers and signs for goods, about 3300 BCE, and bone and ivory labels from a tomb at Abydos in Egypt are among the earliest known writing. Scholars disagree about whether the two systems arose independently or one prompted the other.

label: Stonehenge is built on Salisbury Plain
summary: Stonehenge, a prehistoric megalithic structure on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, begins as a circular earth bank and ditch dated to about 3100 BCE, and activity there continues until about 1600 BCE. Its circle of large sarsen stones is placed between 2600 and 2400 BCE and the smaller bluestones, by radiocarbon dating, between 2400 and 2200 BCE, though they may have been at the site earlier. The monument is aligned with the sunrise on the summer solstice.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Stonehenge

label: Austronesian-speaking seafarers spread from Taiwan across the Pacific and Indian oceans
summary: Most linguists and archaeologists trace the Austronesian languages to Taiwan about 5,000 years ago, and follow their speakers through the Philippines, Island Southeast Asia and Melanesia into the Pacific and westward to Madagascar; Aotearoa is reached about 1250 to 1300 CE. Scholars still debate the routes and the dates.

label: Bantu-speaking peoples spread across central, eastern and southern Africa
summary: Languages of the Bantu family spread out of West Central Africa, from a homeland near the border of Nigeria and Cameroon, beginning about 5,000 years ago by one recent estimate, and over many centuries reached eastern and southern Africa, with farming and ironworking. Language, archaeology and genes give the outline; scholars argue over the start, the routes, the speed, and how far people moved as opposed to ideas.

label: The Caral–Supe civilization builds monumental centres on the coast of Peru
summary: The Caral–Supe, or Norte Chico, civilization of the Peruvian coast is dated between about 3000 and 1800 BCE. Caral, inhabited from about 2600 to 2000 BCE, is the best studied of its sites; its excavators call it the oldest urban centre in the Americas, a claim challenged by finds at nearby Bandurria. UNESCO listed Caral in 2009.

label: Egypt’s Old Kingdom: the age of the pyramids
summary: Kings ruling from Memphis build the first large stone pyramids, at Saqqara and then at Giza. The dates follow a conventional chronology and are uncertain by decades or more.

label: The Indus (Harappan) cities at their height
summary: Planned cities with brick drains, standard weights and carved seals spread across the Indus plain and beyond. Their script has not been deciphered, so what is said of their rulers and beliefs is inferred from what has been dug up.

label: The Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, the Oxus Civilization
summary: The Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, also called the Oxus Civilization, is a Middle Bronze Age civilisation of southern Central Asia around the Caspian and Aral seas that thrived between about 2500 and 1700 BCE (other authors start it about 2300 or 2200 BCE), though there is debate about details and interpretation of the data; some scholars argue that both names are too restrictive. Its people practise irrigation farming of wheat and barley.

label: The Kingdom of Kerma rises on the Nile in Nubia
summary: Kerma, on the Nile in what is now northern Sudan, grows from about 2500 BCE into a large kingdom whose peak is dated between about 1750 and 1500 BCE, when it rivalled Egypt. About 1500 BCE Egypt’s New Kingdom annexes Nubia after campaigns under Thutmose I, though revolts continue for centuries.

label: Sargon founds the Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon takes power in central Mesopotamia, founds a new capital called Akkad and brings the cities of Sumer under one king; the dynasty lasts about 180 years. The site of Akkad has not been found, much of Sargon’s own story comes from later copies and legend, and the dates follow a conventional chronology.

label: A long drought begins about 2200 BCE: the 4.2-kiloyear event
summary: A long drought, one of the most severe climatic events of the Holocene, begins about 2200 BCE and most likely lasts the whole of the 22nd century BCE. It has been hypothesised to have caused the collapse of Egypt’s Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and the Liangzhu culture, and to have helped start the decline of the Indus cities, which some scientists dispute, citing evidence that the event was not a global drought and did not fall in a clear timeframe.

label: Sintashta burials hold the earliest known chariots
summary: The Sintashta culture of the southern Urals is dated to about 2200–1900 BCE; its 23 known fortified settlements show a high level of militarism. The earliest known chariots have been found in Sintashta burials, with chariots appearing in the middle and late phases of the culture, about 2050–1750 BCE; the culture is considered a strong candidate for the origin of the technology, and the page adds that it is widely regarded as the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages.

label: The Minoan palace civilization of Crete
summary: The Minoan civilization, a Bronze Age culture centred on Crete and often regarded as the first civilization in Europe, has complex urban settlements from about 2000 BCE, with palaces at Knossos and Phaistos, and trades widely. After about 1450 BCE it comes under the cultural and perhaps political domination of the Mycenaeans, in a hybrid culture that lasts until about 1100 BCE. Neither of its scripts, Cretan hieroglyphs and Linear A, is fully deciphered.

label: The first alphabets: simple signs for sounds
summary: Short inscriptions from Sinai, which scholars date between about 1850 and 1550 BCE, and later ones from Canaan use a small set of signs for consonants. The Phoenician alphabet, conventionally dated from about 1050 BCE, is the ancestor, directly or through Aramaic, of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

label: The Epic of Gilgamesh takes shape
summary: Poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, are written in Sumerian from about 2100 BCE; an Old Babylonian epic of about 1800 BCE is later reworked into the “standard” version of twelve tablets. Some of the best-preserved copies come from the 7th-century BCE library at Nineveh.

label: Hammurabi rules Babylon; a law code is carved in stone
summary: Hammurabi brings most of Mesopotamia under Babylon’s rule. A stone stele inscribed with about 280 laws, found at Susa in 1901, is the best-known document of his reign. The dates follow the commonly used “middle chronology”; others differ by decades.

label: The Erlitou culture, an early Bronze Age society of the Yellow River valley
summary: The Erlitou culture, named for a site in Henan, is dated by radiocarbon studies since 2007 to about 1750–1500 BCE; earlier estimates gave about 1900 to 1500. Most archaeologists call it the first state-level society in China, and Chinese archaeologists generally identify it with the later part of the Xia dynasty, a link that rests on traditional accounts written much later; some Western scholars argue the link is premature, as no contemporary written records have been found.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Erlitou culture

label: Mycenaean Greece: the palatial states of the Late Bronze Age
summary: Mycenaean Greece, the last phase of the Bronze Age in ancient Greece, spans about 1750 to 1050 BCE, or from about 1700 or 1675 by the page’s own table of the Late Helladic period; the page calls it the first advanced and distinctively Greek civilization on the mainland, with palatial states, urban organization, works of art and a writing system. Its most prominent site is Mycenae, after which the culture is named; other centres include Pylos, Tiryns and Iolcos in Thessaly.

label: Poverty Point: earthen ridges and mounds in the Lower Mississippi valley
summary: Indigenous people of the Late Archaic period build earthen ridges, mounds and a central plaza at Poverty Point in north-eastern Louisiana between about 1700 and 1100 BCE; the earthworks core measures about 345 acres, and the culture’s evidence extends over much of the Southeastern Woodlands. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

label: The Hittite kingdom and empire rule from Hattusa
summary: A king named Labarna takes the name Hattusili I about 1650 BCE and makes Hattusa his capital; the Hittite Empire reaches its peak in the mid-14th century BCE. The earliest written mention of the Hittites is in tablets found at Kanesh with accounts between Assyrian merchants and a “land of Hatti”. The empire ends between about 1200 and 1180 BCE, in the Late Bronze Age collapse, with its capital Hattusa gradually abandoned, and the Hittites splinter into small states.

label: The Thera (Santorini) eruption
summary: One of the largest volcanic eruptions of the last few thousand years buries the town at Akrotiri. Radiocarbon dates, including those from an olive branch buried by the eruption, point to the late 17th or early 16th century BCE, and pottery styles and Egyptian chronology to the mid 16th to early 15th century; a 2018 recalibration moved the radiocarbon range later, but the difference is unresolved. Its effect on Minoan Crete is also debated.

label: The Rhind and Edwin Smith papyri record Egyptian mathematics and surgery
summary: Two papyri of the Second Intermediate Period record Egyptian science. The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, written in the Fifteenth Dynasty, is presented by the scribe Ahmes as “accurate reckoning for inquiring into things”. The Edwin Smith Papyrus, a text on trauma surgery, describes 48 cases of injuries, fractures, wounds, dislocations and tumours; its copy dates to about 1600 BCE, though the original may date from the Old Kingdom.

label: Lapita seafarers settle Island Melanesia and reach Fiji, Tonga and Samoa
summary: The Lapita culture, a Neolithic Austronesian people with distinctive stamped pottery, settles Island Melanesia by sea at around 1600 to 500 BCE, and its range stretches more than 4,000 km to Fiji and Tonga, with its most eastern limit in Samoa. Lapita pottery from around 1000 BCE has been found in Fiji, and uranium–thorium dates put the first Lapita landfall in Tonga, at Nukuleka, at about 890 BCE. The Lapita people are believed to have come from the northern Philippines.

label: The Shang dynasty on the Yellow River plain
summary: Kings of the Shang rule from a series of capitals, the last at Anyang, where bronze vessels and inscribed oracle bones were found. The bones, from about 1250 BCE, carry the earliest known Chinese writing. The date of the dynasty’s beginning is a rough estimate.

label: Egypt’s New Kingdom: an empire from Nubia to the Levant
summary: After the Hyksos rulers are driven out, the kings of the 18th to 20th dynasties campaign in Nubia and the Levant and build great temples at Thebes. Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II belong to this age.

label: The Nok culture makes terracotta figures in central Nigeria
summary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria is known from terracotta figures first found in 1928 near the village of Nok, and from settlement sites with ironworking and farming remains. Dates are still being refined: one account gives about 1500 BCE to the 1st century BCE, with the earliest terracottas perhaps about 900 BCE and iron metallurgy, which may have arisen independently, between about 750 and 550 BCE.

label: The Rigveda, a collection of Vedic hymns, is composed
summary: The Rigveda, a collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns, is composed in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, most likely between about 1500 and 1000 BCE; a wider range of about 1900 to 1200 BCE has also been given. Scholars date it from its language and contents, not from a dated record, and most believe its hymns were handed down orally with great fidelity from the 2nd millennium BCE.

label: The Amarna letters: the diplomatic correspondence of Egypt and its neighbours on clay tablets
summary: The Amarna letters are an archive on clay tablets, mainly diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian administration and its representatives in Canaan and Amurru or the leaders of neighbouring kingdoms, spanning no more than 30 years in the middle of the 14th century BCE. They were found at el-Amarna, the site of Akhenaten’s capital Akhetaten; most are in a variety of Akkadian sometimes described as a mixed Canaanite-Akkadian, and the known tablets total 382.

label: A ship carrying goods from many lands sinks off southern Turkey
summary: The wreck, found in 1982, held copper and tin ingots, glass ingots, ivory, ebony and goods from Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus, the Aegean and Mesopotamia. It shows how far Late Bronze Age trade reached; the date is worked out from tree rings and radiocarbon.

label: The Battle of Kadesh and the first well-preserved peace treaty
summary: Egyptian and Hittite armies meet near Kadesh in about 1274 BCE (some chronologies put it about twenty years earlier), and each king claims victory. About 1259 BCE they make a treaty, of which Egyptian and Hittite versions survive: the oldest well-preserved peace treaty.

label: Chavín de Huántar, an Andean ceremonial centre
summary: Chavín de Huántar, in the Andes of Peru, is built in stages from before 1200 BCE, with most major construction done by about 750 BCE and use as a ceremonial centre until about 500 BCE. Its central Lanzón gallery holds a carved stone figure taken to be its chief deity. UNESCO lists the site.

label: Ironworking spreads across Asia, Europe and Africa
summary: Smiths in Anatolia, the Near East and elsewhere learn to make and work iron in quantity, and by about 1000 BCE iron tools and weapons are in use from Greece to India; iron working is found in sub-Saharan Africa by the first millennium BCE. Whether it was invented once or several times is debated.

label: The Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a generation or two many cities of the eastern Mediterranean, including Hattusa and Ugarit, are destroyed or abandoned, and trade networks break. Earthquakes, drought, migrations, revolt and invasion have all been proposed as causes; no single explanation is agreed.

label: Olmec centres on the Gulf coast of Mexico
summary: San Lorenzo and later La Venta are early centres with large earth platforms and carved stone heads. They are often called the earliest civilization of Mesoamerica; some scholars see them as one among several interacting early cultures.

label: Sanxingdui: bronze masks and figures of a Bronze Age culture in Sichuan
summary: Sanxingdui, in Guanghan, Sichuan, was largely discovered in 1986 after a preliminary find in 1927. Radiocarbon dating places its artifacts, among them bronzes, in the 12th–11th centuries BCE; archaeologists have identified the locale with the ancient kingdom of Shu.

label: The Zhou dynasty replaces the Shang and introduces the Mandate of Heaven
summary: The Zhou dynasty rules from about 1046 BCE (some scholars give 1045) until 256 BCE, when the state of Qin formally ends it: the Western Zhou to 771 BCE, the Eastern Zhou after that, its authority increasingly ceremonial. Its rulers introduce the Mandate of Heaven, an idea of rule that later dynasties take up. One reference states that it lasted 790 years, the longest span of any dynasty in Chinese history.

label: The Đông Sơn bronze-drum culture of northern Vietnam
summary: The Đông Sơn culture is a Bronze Age culture centred on the Red River Delta in northern Vietnam, named for the bronze drums first excavated in Thanh Hóa province in 1924. Its artifacts, or ones closely related, are found from about 1000 BCE to the 1st century CE as far as Malaysia, Laos and the Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guangxi and Fujian.

label: The Garamantes build a Saharan kingdom on foggara irrigation
summary: The Garamantes, who may have descended from Berber and Saharan pastoralist peoples, settle in the Fezzan region of Libya at least as early as 1000 BCE and establish a civilization that flourishes until its end in the late 7th century CE. Their agriculture rests on an extensive system of qanat irrigation, the foggaras; their largest town, Garama, has about four thousand people, with some six thousand more in its suburbs.

label: The Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: Assyrian kings, from their cities on the upper Tigris, conquer lands from Egypt to Iran and move large populations from place to place. Nineveh falls to Babylonian and Median armies in 612 BCE, and the last Assyrian force is defeated in 609.

label: The Etruscans build a federation of city-states in Italy
summary: A civilization that is identifiably Etruscan dates from about 900 BCE, in the Iron Age Villanovan culture of Etruria, in what is now Tuscany, western Umbria and northern Lazio, and forms a federation of city-states with a common language and culture. The Etruscans write in a script derived from the Euboean alphabet. From the late 4th century BCE they succumb to the expanding Rome in the Roman–Etruscan Wars, and they are granted Roman citizenship in 90 BCE.

label: Carthage is founded and Phoenician trade spreads west
summary: The Greek historian Timaeus gave 814 BCE as the year settlers from Tyre founded Carthage, in what is now Tunisia. Greek pottery from the earliest levels found there is dated to about 760 BCE, while radiocarbon dates on animal bones from the lowest levels fall in the late 9th to 8th centuries BCE; scholars differ on how to reconcile them with the traditional date.

label: The Scythians dominate the Pontic steppe
summary: The Scythians, an Eastern Iranic nomadic people skilled in mounted warfare, migrate in the 9th to 8th centuries BCE from Central Asia to the Pontic steppe, displace the Agathyrsi and the Cimmerians, and remain until the 3rd century BCE. Much of what is written about them comes from Greek authors, above all Herodotus, whose account is mixed with folklore and is less reliable. Darius I attacks their kingdom in 513 BCE.

label: The ancient Olympic Games are held at Olympia
summary: The ancient Olympic Games, athletic competitions among the city-states at the sanctuary of Olympia in honour of Zeus, are traditionally dated to 776 BCE and held every four years, an Olympiad that becomes a unit of time in Greek history. Their last recorded celebration is in 393 CE under the emperor Theodosius I, though archaeological evidence indicates that some games were held later; they likely ended under Theodosius II, possibly after a fire at the temple of Zeus.

Causes proposed include strong economic growth and consequent overpopulation of the home states, and drought; Herodotus gives two different accounts of the founding of one colony.

label: The Iliad and the Odyssey are composed in Greek
summary: Two long poems about the Trojan War and its aftermath, attributed to Homer, take shape out of a long oral tradition and are written down about the 8th or 7th century BCE. Whether one poet made both, and when each reached its present form, has been debated since antiquity.

label: Kings from Kush rule Egypt as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty
summary: Kings from Kush, in the Nile valley of what is now northern Sudan, rule all or part of Egypt from about 744 to 656 BCE. Piye records his campaign into Lower Egypt on the Victory Stela. Assyrian armies under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal later defeat the dynasty and the Late Period begins; recent work puts Shabaka after Shebitku, reversing the older order.

label: Lydia makes coins of electrum at Sardis
summary: In Lydia, in western Anatolia, with its capital at Sardis, coins of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, are struck from about the 7th century BCE; they are among the oldest in existence, with dates for the first coins ranging from about 700 to 550 BCE, and the most common opinion places them at or near the start of King Alyattes’s reign. The Lydians are known in part for early coinage; Lydia becomes a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire in 546 BCE.

label: Meroë becomes the capital of the Kingdom of Kush
summary: Meroë, on the east bank of the Nile in what is now Sudan, is the capital of the Kingdom of Kush for several centuries from about 590 BCE until the kingdom’s collapse in the 4th century CE. The site has more than two hundred pyramids in three groups; the region was rich in iron ore and hardwood for ironworking, and the city lay on routes to the Red Sea.

label: Cyrus takes Babylon; the Persian (Achaemenid) Empire
summary: Cyrus conquers Media and Lydia and, in 539 BCE, Babylon; his successors extend the empire from Egypt to the Indus. A clay cylinder from Babylon, written in Cyrus’s name, gives an account of the conquest. The Hebrew Bible (Ezra 1) reports that he let exiled Judeans go home; the Cylinder names Mesopotamian sanctuaries and does not mention the Judeans.

label: The Behistun inscription: Darius records his reign in three languages
summary: Darius the Great (r. 522–486 BCE) has a multilingual royal inscription and rock relief carved on a cliff at Behistun in western Iran, the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Grotefend had read ten of the 37 Old Persian signs by 1802; Henry Rawlinson began to study the inscription in 1835 and sent a full copy to Europe in 1847, which helped decipher cuneiform.

label: The Roman Republic replaces the monarchy
summary: The Roman Republic begins with the overthrow of the Roman Kingdom, traditionally dated to 509 BCE, and ends in 27 BCE with the establishment of the Roman Empire after the War of Actium. In this period Rome’s control expands from the city’s immediate surroundings to hegemony over the entire Mediterranean world.

label: Cleisthenes’ reforms at Athens: rule by the citizens’ assembly
summary: After the Peisistratid family is driven from power, the statesman Cleisthenes reorganises the citizens into ten new tribes, with a council of 500, and gives the Assembly real power. Only free adult men born to citizen parents take part; women, enslaved people and foreigners are excluded.

label: The Hundred Schools of Thought flourish in China

label: Monte Albán, the Zapotec centre of the Valley of Oaxaca
summary: Founded toward the end of the Middle Formative period at around 500 BCE, Monte Albán is for nearly a thousand years the pre-eminent Zapotec socio-political and economic centre, on a low range above the Valley of Oaxaca. label: The Nazca lines are drawn in the desert of southern Peru
summary: People of the Paracas phase (400 to 200 BCE) and then the Nazca phase (200 BCE to 500 CE) make geoglyphs in the soil of the Nazca Desert by removing pebbles to leave different-coloured dirt exposed; several hundred new figures have been found in the 21st century. Scholars differ in interpreting the purpose of the designs but in general ascribe religious significance to them. They were designated a World Heritage Site in 1994.

label: The Pazyryk burials preserve a Scythian-type culture of the Altai in ice
summary: The Pazyryk burials are Scythian (Saka) Iron Age tombs in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, dated chiefly to the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, with some of the 5th. Because of a climatic freeze, goods in the tombs stayed frozen in the permafrost until their excavation, among them felt hangings, Chinese silk, the earliest known pile carpet and horses fitted with elaborate harness.

summary: According to the Roman historians’ accounts, such as Livy’s, written a couple of centuries later, a first board of ten men (decemviri) is appointed about 450 BCE to draw up the laws, a second completes the last two tables, and the Twelve Tables are promulgated in 449 BCE; scholars do not agree on the exact account. summary: The Parthenon, a temple of the goddess Athena on the Acropolis, is built in the 5th century BCE in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the Persian invaders. Construction starts in 447 BCE, when the Delian League is at the peak of its power, the building is completed in 438 BCE, and work on its sculptures and decoration continues until 432 BCE. For a time it serves as the treasury of the Delian League.

summary: Meton of Athens introduces a 19-year cycle to the Attic calendar in 432 BCE, after which the lunar phases recur at the same time of the year; he judges the cycle to be a whole number of days, 6,940. Our report of it comes from a later writer, Diodorus Siculus, who says that Meton fixed its beginning on the thirteenth day of the month Scirophorion.

label: The Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and its allies fight Sparta and its allies for 27 years, with the plague of Athens, a failed Athenian expedition to Sicily, and, in the end, Athens’s defeat. Our main account is by Thucydides, who took part.

sources.title: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War

causes.note: Thucydides names the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta; modern historians discuss other causes.
Trade and tribute are argued about as causes.

label: The Hippocratic Corpus gathers early Greek medical writing
summary: The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around 60 early Greek medical works closely associated with the physician Hippocrates and his teachings, most of them from the last decades of the 5th century BCE and the first half of the 4th. It covers many aspects of medicine, from theories of illness to ethical conduct, and includes the Hippocratic Oath.

label: The plague of Athens
summary: A disease breaks out in crowded Athens in the second year of the war with Sparta and returns twice. Thucydides, who caught it and survived, describes its symptoms. It killed a large share of the city’s people, but ancient numbers are uncertain and modern scholars have proposed several diseases without agreeing on one.

sources.title: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book II

label: Babylonian astronomers divide the ecliptic into twelve equal signs
summary: About the end of the 5th century BCE Babylonian astronomers divide the ecliptic into twelve equal “signs” of 30 degrees each, by analogy with twelve months of 30 days. The date rests on modern astronomical calculation, which places the introduction of the zodiac between 409 and 398 BCE, during Persian rule, and probably within a few years of 401 BCE; the earliest extant Greek text using the division is by Hypsicles of Alexandria, about 190 BCE.

label: Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī sets out the grammar of Sanskrit

places.name: Gandhara (Salatura, named in later sources as Pāṇini’s home)

summary: Pāṇini, whom later sources call a man of Salatura in Gandhara, composes the Aṣṭādhyāyī, a grammar of Sanskrit in 3,959 rules (sūtras) arranged in eight chapters; it is the earliest Sanskrit grammar that survives intact. Nothing is known of his life beyond what can be inferred from his work and legends recorded long after, and scholars date him variously between the 6th–5th and the 4th centuries BCE, some from the coins his rules name to the mid-4th century.

label: The Mahabharata and the Ramayana take shape
summary: The two great Sanskrit epics of India reach their present form over centuries from oral tradition. The bulk of the Mahabharata was probably compiled between the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, its oldest preserved parts not much older than about 400 BCE; for the Ramayana, estimates of the composition range from the 8th–5th to the 5th–4th centuries BCE, with later additions to the 3rd century CE. Scholars debate the layers of each.

label: Plato founds the Academy at Athens
summary: Plato, a pupil of Socrates, who was tried and put to death in 399 BCE, sets up a school outside Athens that lasts in several forms for centuries. His dialogues shape later Greek, Jewish, Christian and Muslim thought.

label: Pytheas of Massalia sails to northern Europe
summary: Pytheas, a Greek geographer and explorer from the colony of Massalia, makes a voyage of exploration to northern Europe in about 325 BCE. His account, widely known in antiquity, has not survived and is known only through the writings of others, among them Strabo; he introduced the idea of distant Thule to the geographic imagination.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pytheas
sources.note: read: his dates, the voyage, the lost account and the authors who report it

label: The Hellenistic kingdoms follow Alexander the Great
summary: The Hellenistic period, from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE to the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BCE, is one in which Greek and eastern Mediterranean and West Asian lands are under the influence of Greek leadership, culture and language as a result of Alexander’s conquests. Kingdoms are established in West Asia (the Seleucid Empire and the Kingdom of Pergamon) and in north-east Africa (the Ptolemaic Kingdom); the Roman conquest of Egypt in 30 BCE ends the last major one.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hellenistic period
sources.note: read: the dates, the kingdoms, the end of the Ptolemaic kingdom

related.note: The Library of Alexandria belongs to the Ptolemaic kingdom; its end is disputed.

label: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
summary: Chandragupta Maurya founds a geographically extensive empire in South Asia with its power base in Magadha and its capital at Pataliputra, about 320 BCE, and it holds together loosely until 185 BCE. The main written sources are partial quotations of Megasthenes’s lost history in Roman texts of several centuries later, and the Edicts of Ashoka.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Maurya Empire
sources.note: read: the founding, the capital, the sources and the end of the dynasty

label: Euclid’s Elements: geometry built from definitions and proofs
summary: Euclid of Alexandria sets out Greek geometry in thirteen books, deriving each result step by step from definitions and a few starting assumptions. It was a standard textbook for over two thousand years.

label: Sangam literature: the earliest known literature of South India
summary: The early classical Tamil poems known as Sangam literature, which belong to Tamilakam (Tamil Nadu, Kerala and parts of Sri Lanka), are called the earliest known literature of South India. Scholars differ on the dates: most place the Sangam period from about 300 BCE to 300 CE, others later and more narrowly but before 300 CE. They regard the Tamil tradition’s chronology of three academies lasting thousands of years as mythical.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sangam literature
sources.note: read in full: the dating, the anthologies, the legendary academies

label: The Library and Museum of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemaic kings of Egypt found a library and a research institution at Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE and gather scrolls from across the Mediterranean world. How and when it declined is disputed: a fire at the harbour in 48 BCE, the fighting of the 270s CE and the destruction of its daughter library, the Serapeum, in 391 CE have all been named, and the accounts of a burning were written decades or centuries later.

sources.title: Roger S. Bagnall, ‘Alexandria: Library of Dreams’, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 146 (2002)
sources.note: on how little is known of its founding and its end

label: Ashoka rules the Maurya Empire
summary: Ashoka rules most of the Indian subcontinent. His edicts, carved on rocks and pillars, are the earliest long readable inscriptions of India; they describe his regret after the war in Kalinga and a policy of “dhamma” that includes respect for the different sects.

sources.title: Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict XIII and others)
sources.note: in the Library: two translations

label: The Punic Wars between Rome and Carthage
summary: Three wars over Sicily, Spain and the western Mediterranean end with Rome destroying Carthage in 146 BCE and taking its lands. Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps in 218 BCE is the best-known episode.

causes.note: Rivalry for Sicily and then for Spain and the western Mediterranean.
Control of trade routes and tribute is said to have mattered; our main accounts are Roman and Greek.

label: Eratosthenes calculates the circumference of the Earth
summary: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, later chief librarian at Alexandria, is best remembered as the first known person to calculate the circumference of the Earth. His own account has not survived, and the method rests on a simplified version by Cleomedes: at noon on the summer solstice rods cast no shadow at Syene (Aswan) but do at Alexandria, and Cleomedes says that Eratosthenes measured the shadow’s angle at about 7.2 degrees.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Eratosthenes
sources.note: read: his life, the measurement of the Earth, Cleomedes’s account

label: Kush writes its own language in the Meroitic scripts
summary: From the 3rd century BCE the Kingdom of Kush writes its own language in two scripts, a cursive derived from Egyptian Demotic and a hieroglyphic form derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs. Francis Llewellyn Griffith deciphered the script in 1909, from the Meroitic spellings of Egyptian names, but the Meroitic language itself remains poorly understood. The last known inscription is dated to the 5th century CE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Meroitic script
sources.note: read in full: the two scripts, Griffith’s decipherment, the last inscription

label: The Parthian Empire rules Iran and Mesopotamia on the Silk Road
summary: Arsaces I, leader of the Parni tribe, founds the Parthian, or Arsacid, Empire in 247 BCE after conquering Parthia (some scholars place the conquest about 238 BCE); Mithridates I (r. about 171–132 BCE) takes Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids. Lying on the Silk Road between Rome and Han China, the empire becomes a centre of trade and commerce; the seat of government moves from Nisa to Ctesiphon, and the empire lasts until 224 CE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Parthian Empire
sources.note: read: the founding, the expansion, the Silk Road, the capital

label: Qin unifies China; the title of emperor is taken
summary: King Zheng of Qin finishes conquering the other warring states in 221 BCE and takes the title Shi Huangdi, “first emperor”. The state standardises weights, measures, coinage and writing; the dynasty ends in 206 BCE.

label: The Terracotta Army is buried with Qin Shi Huang

places.name: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, Lintong

summary: A collection of terracotta sculptures depicting armies is buried with Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, in 210–209 BCE to protect him in the afterlife. Farmers digging a well found the figures on 29 March 1974; estimates from 2007 were that the three pits hold more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses and 150 cavalry horses.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Terracotta Army
sources.note: read: the burial, the discovery of 1974, the estimates of 2007

label: The Xiongnu form a steppe empire under Modu
summary: The Xiongnu, a tribal confederation of nomadic peoples known from Chinese sources, inhabit the eastern Eurasian steppe from the 3rd century BCE to the late 1st century CE. Modu Chanyu, their leader from 209 BCE, founds the Xiongnu Empire after overthrowing their overlords the Yuezhi, and they become the dominant power on the steppes, centred on the Mongolian Plateau.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Xiongnu
sources.note: read: the origin, Modu, the dates of the confederation

label: The Han dynasty
summary: A four-century dynasty, with a break from 9 to 25 CE, that sets a lasting pattern of imperial government. The court under Emperor Wu supports Confucian learning and opens routes to Central Asia; Buddhism first reaches China in this period.

label: The Arthashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, is compiled

places.name: Pataliputra (Magadha; the place of composition is not known)

summary: The Arthashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, economic policy and war, is traditionally ascribed to Kautilya, the counsellor of Chandragupta Maurya. Scholars disagree about its date and authorship but see the work of several authors over centuries: Olivelle dates the earlier treatises it draws on from the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE, and McClish and Olivelle its compilation to the 1st century CE and a major expansion to the 2nd or 3rd century CE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arthashastra
sources.note: read in full: the dating by Olivelle, McClish and others, the question of Kautilya’s authorship, the manuscripts

label: The Antikythera mechanism: a geared device for the sky
summary: A corroded bronze device recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck found in 1900 has about thirty surviving gears and seems to model the movements of the sun and moon and to predict eclipses. Estimates of its date run from about 205 BCE to about 87 BCE (the wreck itself is dated to about 70 to 60 BCE), and its maker is not known.

label: Paper is made in China
summary: Fragments of paper from tombs in northern China date from the 2nd century BCE. A later account says the court official Cai Lun presented an improved paper to the emperor in 105 CE; scholars differ on how much to credit him, since earlier paper existed.

label: Zhang Qian’s missions open routes between China and Central Asia
summary: The Han envoy Zhang Qian travels west to seek allies against the Xiongnu and returns with reports of Ferghana, Bactria and Parthia. His journeys lead to regular contact and trade along the routes later called the Silk Road, which also carry ideas and faiths.

sources.title: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, chapter 123

label: The Silk Road links East and West
summary: The Silk Road, a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century, spans over 6,400 km on land and plays a central role in economic, cultural, political and religious exchange between East and West. The name was coined only in the late 19th century, and some historians prefer “Silk Routes”; it derives from the trade in silk textiles, chiefly from China, and the explorations of the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian opened the way.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silk Road
sources.note: read: the definition, the dates, the origin of the name, Zhang Qian

label: Hipparchus discovers the precession of the equinoxes
summary: Hipparchus, a Greek astronomer, is generally recognised as the discoverer of the precession of the equinoxes, in 127 BCE. The account rests on Ptolemy’s Almagest, which mentions his two books on precession and reports that he measured the longitudes of Spica, Regulus and other bright stars and could not reconcile his data with the earlier observations of Timocharis and Aristillus.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hipparchus

label: The Charaka and Sushruta compendia set out Ayurvedic medicine

places.name: Northern India (place of composition not known)

summary: Two Sanskrit compendia are foundational texts of Ayurveda: the Charaka Samhita, which presents theories of physiology, diagnosis and the three humours, and the Sushruta Samhita, which includes chapters on surgical procedures. Their dates are debated: one history of Indian medical literature places Charaka’s compilation between 100 BCE and 200 CE, with a revision by Dṛḍhabala dated to the 6th century CE, and a date of about 600 BCE for the Sushruta text has been challenged.

label: The Hopewell exchange network links the Eastern Woodlands
summary: The Hopewell tradition, in the Middle Woodland period, is a network of precontact Native American cultures in settlements along rivers in the northeastern and midwestern Eastern Woodlands from about 100 BCE to 500 CE. It was not a single culture or society but a widely dispersed set of populations connected by a common network of trade routes; graves hold ornaments of copper, mica and obsidian imported from hundreds of miles away.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hopewell tradition
sources.note: read: the definition, the dates, the trade goods in the graves

label: Sima Qian writes the Records of the Grand Historian
summary: Sima Qian, an early Han historian, writes the Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian, in the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE, building on work begun by his father Sima Tan. It is the first of the Twenty-Four Histories of imperial China and covers a period of 2,500 years, from the age of the legendary Yellow Emperor to his own time.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Shiji
sources.note: read: the authorship, the dates, the scope

label: Teotihuacan grows into a city of the Valley of Mexico
summary: A city grows from about 100 BCE in the Valley of Mexico, 40 km north-east of today’s Mexico City, around the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon. Estimates of its population run from at least 25,000 to about 100,000 at its height, and the page also gives 100,000 to 200,000 for about 400–500 CE. Its major monuments are sacked and burned about 550 CE; its collapse may be related to the extreme weather of 535–536.

label: Julius Caesar reforms the Roman calendar
summary: Julius Caesar proposes in 46 BCE a solar calendar of 365 days with a day added every fourth year, to replace the Roman calendar whose months the pontiffs had let drift from the seasons by adding months or days at will. To bring the new year of 1 January into line with the seasons, 46 BCE is made 445 days long, and the Julian calendar begins on 1 January 45 BCE; Sosigenes of Alexandria is generally considered its principal designer.

label: The Long Count calendar is carved on monuments in Mesoamerica
summary: The Long Count counts days from a mythical creation date that corresponds to 11 August 3114 BCE. The earliest contemporaneous Long Count inscription yet discovered is on Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo in Chiapas, read as 36 BCE, though that date is not certain; Stela 2 from Takalik Abaj in Guatemala may be earlier, but its battered inscription remains controversial.

label: Augustus becomes the first Roman emperor
summary: In 27 BCE the Senate gives Octavian the name Augustus, and one man holds the chief powers of the Roman state. Emperors rule the Roman world, in the east until 1453.

label: Funan, a network of early states on the Mekong delta
summary: Funan is a loose network of Indianized states in mainland Southeast Asia, covering parts of present-day Cambodia, Thailand and Vietnam, which existed from the 1st to the 7th century CE. Goods excavated at Óc Eo in southern Vietnam show that it was a trading state. The name Funan comes from Chinese texts and does not appear in locally produced texts of the period.

label: The Kushan Empire spans Bactria, Gandhara and northern India
summary: The Kushan Empire, formed by the Yuezhi in the early 1st century CE, begins in Bactria and spreads over much of what is now Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India, reaching Sarnath near Varanasi. Its rulers put the name Koshano on their coins in Greek letters, and inscriptions in Sanskrit in the Brahmi script call the emperor Kushana. It is dated from about 30 to about 375 CE.

label: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art reaches its final stage
summary: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, a Chinese mathematics book composed by several generations of scholars, by the page’s account from the 10th to the 2nd century BCE, reaches its latest stage in the 1st century CE; it is one of the earliest surviving mathematical texts from China. Liu Hui writes a detailed commentary in 263; its method in chapter 8 resembles Gaussian elimination, and it uses red and black rods for positive and negative numbers.

label: A Greek merchant’s handbook describes sea trade from Egypt to India
summary: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, written in Greek in the first century CE by an unknown author, thought to have been a seafarer or trader of Roman Egypt, lists ports, goods and rulers from the Red Sea to East Africa and India and mentions the use of the monsoon winds.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

label: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum
summary: An eruption covers the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum in ash and hot gas. Pliny the Younger describes it in letters to Tacitus. The towns, uncovered from the 18th century, show daily life, including temples and shrines of several gods. The traditional date is 24 August; some finds suggest it may have been later in the autumn.

label: The Kingdom of Aksum, a trading power of the Red Sea
summary: From its highland capital Aksum links trade between the Roman world, Arabia and India, mints its own coins and raises tall carved stelae. Its king Ezana adopts Christianity in the 4th century. The kingdom declines from the 7th century, and dates for its end vary.

label: Zhang Heng presents a seismoscope to the Han court
summary: Zhang Heng, a polymath and Chief Astronomer of the Eastern Han, introduces to the court in 132 an intricate seismoscope which, he claimed, could detect the direction of a distant earthquake; on one occasion it indicated an earthquake in the northwest, and a later report placed it in Gansu, some 400 to 500 km northwest of Luoyang. He is also credited with a water-powered armillary sphere and with improved calculations of pi.

label: Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos sets out a system of astrology
summary: Claudius Ptolemy, a scholar of Alexandria, writes the Tetrabiblos, “four books”, a text on the philosophy and practice of astrology, in Greek in the 2nd century CE; it is the companion of his astronomical Almagest. Its astrology continued to be taught at European universities in the Renaissance and early modern period.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tetrabiblos
sources.note: read: the author, the date, the contents, its later use

label: The Antonine Plague
summary: A pandemic reaches the Roman Empire, said to have been brought by soldiers returning from campaigns in the east, and recurs for years; the physician Galen describes it. It may have been smallpox or measles. Estimates of the dead differ greatly, and some historians put them at several million.

label: Tiwanaku becomes a power in the Titicaca basin
summary: Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca in what is now Bolivia, is founded about 110 CE by one statistical assessment of radiocarbon dates, gains power in the basin between 200 and 500, and peaks between 500 and 600. A conservative estimate gives 10,000 to 20,000 people about 800. The society appears to have collapsed about 1000; the reason is debated, and evidence of drought is one proposal.

label: The Sasanian Empire succeeds the Parthians in Iran
summary: Ardashir I is crowned at Ctesiphon in 224 and takes the title shahanshah, “king of kings”; the House of Sasan rules the Iranian world until 651. Its capital stays at Ctesiphon for all but the first two years, and its rulers revitalise Zoroastrianism as a legitimising and unifying ideal. Its rule over ancient Iran lasts over four centuries, second only in length to that of the Parthian dynasty before it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sasanian Empire
sources.note: read: the founding, the capital, the role of Zoroastrianism, the end in 651

label: The Plague of Cyprian afflicts the Roman Empire
summary: A pandemic afflicts the Roman Empire from about 249 to 262, or from 251/2 to 270 by another reckoning, and is thought to have caused widespread shortages of manpower for food production and the army during the Crisis of the Third Century. It is named for Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who described it. The pathogen is uncertain, since it has not been identified: smallpox, measles and a viral haemorrhagic fever such as Ebola have been proposed; at its height 5,000 people a day were said to be dying in Rome.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Plague of Cyprian

label: Classic Maya cities, writing and astronomy
summary: Kings of city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán record their reigns and rituals in carved stone texts, in a script largely deciphered since the 1980s, and keep a precise calendar.

label: The Gupta Empire
summary: Gupta kings rule much of northern India. Sanskrit literature, mathematics and astronomy and temple building flourish, and the Chinese pilgrim Faxian travels through the empire around 400 CE.

label: Constantine refounds Byzantium as Constantinople
summary: The Roman emperor Constantine I refounds the existing city of Byzantium in 324, at first as Nova Roma, “New Rome”; in 330 it becomes the new eastern capital of the Roman Empire. It is the capital of the Roman and then the Byzantine Empire until the Ottoman takeover of 1453 (apart from the Latin Empire, 1204–1261), and then of the Ottoman Empire until the abolition of the sultanate in 1922.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Constantinople
sources.note: read: the refoundation of 324, the capital from 330, the later capitals

label: The First Council of Nicaea mandates a uniform date for Easter
summary: The Roman emperor Constantine I convenes a council of Christian bishops at Nicaea, now İznik, that meets from May to the end of July 325 and is attended by at least 200 bishops, almost all from the eastern half of the empire. Its main acts are the settlement of the dispute between Arius and Alexander of Alexandria over the nature of the Son, the first part of the Nicene Creed, the mandating of uniform observance of the date of Easter, and early canon law.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First Council of Nicaea

label: Augustine argues from twins against astrological prediction
summary: In the Confessions, which he writes in Latin between 397 and 400, Augustine of Hippo recalls his belief in astrology and gives an argument against it: twins are born so close together that an astrologer’s figures cannot tell them apart, yet the same figures would have foretold the same for Esau and Jacob, to whom it did not happen, so an astrologer who speaks truly speaks by chance, not by art.

label: Nalanda, a Buddhist monastic centre of learning in Magadha
summary: Nalanda, a Buddhist monastery (mahavihara) in Magadha, now in Bihar, is established about 427 CE by the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I and over some 750 years its faculty includes leading scholars of Mahayana Buddhism; Xuanzang is one of its students. Sanskrit texts reach East Asia through pilgrims such as Xuanzang and Yijing. It is raided and burned about 1200 by forces of Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, on the evidence of ash and Tibetan records, but may have continued for decades or longer. UNESCO lists the site.

label: The Western Roman Empire ends
summary: In 476 the commander Odoacer removes the last emperor in the west, Romulus Augustulus. Historians use the year as a convenient marker: daily life changed gradually, and the Roman Empire went on in the east for almost a thousand years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

label: Madagascar is settled from Borneo and East Africa
summary: Madagascar is settled in waves of people of diverse origins, from South Borneo in Indonesia and from East Africa, primarily Austronesian and Bantu; the Malagasy language is Austronesian with Bantu, French and Arabic influences. The earliest unambiguous evidence of continuous human presence, at Andavakoera, dates to 490 CE; earlier dates have been claimed and brief visits cannot be ruled out, so the date of first settlement is uncertain.

label: Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya at Kusumapura
summary: Aryabhata, who called himself a native of Kusumapura (Pataliputra, near Patna), writes the Aryabhatiya, a work of mathematics and astronomy. It states that he was 23 years old in the year 3600 of the Kali Yuga, which corresponds to 499 CE and implies a birth in 476, though the page notes that this does not mean the text was composed in that year.

label: Sogdian merchants carry the Silk Road trade
summary: The Sogdians, an eastern Iranian people between the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya centred on Samarkand, play an essential role as middlemen in the Silk Road trade between China, the Sasanian Empire and the Byzantine Empire; their merchants and diplomats travel as far west as Byzantium. They first practise Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism and Buddhism, and the Muslim conquest of Transoxiana in the 8th century brings their conversion to Islam.

label: Dionysius Exiguus devises the Anno Domini era
summary: The Eastern Roman monk Dionysius Exiguus devises in Rome in 525 the anno Domini dating system, counting years from the traditional year of the conception or birth of Jesus, to number the years of his Easter table; it replaces the Diocletian era of older Easter tables. It is not widely used until the 9th century.

label: Justinian’s Corpus Juris Civilis gathers Roman law
summary: Emperor Justinian has jurists collect and edit centuries of Roman law, with the Code, the Digest and the Institutes finished by 534. It becomes a basis for legal systems in much of Europe and later elsewhere.

label: Justinian builds the church of Hagia Sophia
summary: The Byzantine emperor Justinian I builds the Christian basilica of Hagia Sophia between 532 and 537, after the previous church on the site was destroyed in the Nika riots; it is the third church built there. The page says that it became the world’s largest interior space and among the first buildings to use a fully pendentive dome. It remained a church until 1453.

label: The volcanic winter of 536

places.name: Northern Hemisphere (sites of the eruptions uncertain)

summary: In early 536, or possibly late 535, an eruption of uncertain location puts great amounts of sulfate aerosols into the air; at least three eruptions in all bring one of the most severe and protracted coolings of the Northern Hemisphere in two thousand years. Procopius and Cassiodorus describe the dimmed sun, snow is reported in China in August, and the page links the cooling with crop failures, famine and the Plague of Justinian.

label: The Plague of Justinian
summary: Plague reaches Constantinople in 542 and recurs around the Mediterranean world for two centuries. DNA from burials confirms that the cause was the plague bacterium, Yersinia pestis. How many died, and what effect it had on the empire, are still debated.

label: The First Turkic Khaganate rules the steppe
summary: The Ashina clan of the Göktürks, under Bumin Qaghan (d. 552) and his brother Istämi, founds the First Turkic Khaganate, succeeding the Rouran as the hegemonic power of the Mongolian Plateau; its official texts and coins are written in Sogdian, and it is the first Turkic state to use the name Türk politically. It collapses in 603 after conflicts and civil wars, dividing into the Eastern and Western khaganates, which Tang China conquers in 630 and later.

label: Khipu: record-keeping with knotted cords in the Andes
summary: A khipu (quipu) is a record-keeping device of knotted cords used by various cultures in the central Andes, most prominently by the Inca Empire; the first undisputed evidence dates to the Middle Horizon, about 600–1000 CE, probably from the Wari Empire. Colour, order and number carry its information; specialist officials read them. Numbers can be read, but how non-numeric information is encoded is disputed, and one claim of a phonetic decipherment rests on khipus of the colonial period.

summary: A political formation centred on the Ayacucho Basin of Peru emerges about 600 CE and grows to cover much of the coastal and highland country, in the same centuries as Tiwanaku. Its decline begins about the 10th century and its end is dated to about 1000 or 1100. Archaeologists once thought it derived from Tiwanaku; a Wari city found near Chiclayo in 2008 shows how far north it reached.

label: China begins to choose officials by written examination
summary: The idea of choosing bureaucrats by merit rather than birth begins early in Chinese history; the first earnest use of written examinations for recruitment comes under the Sui dynasty, with 605 given as the origin of the imperial examination and 607 by many as its real beginning. The Tang make it a regular channel for appointment. It lasts until its abolition in the late Qing reforms of 1905.

summary: Sections of what is now the Grand Canal date from the early 5th century BCE, when the Han Canal was begun in 486 BCE to link the Yangtze with the Huai. Emperor Yang of Sui expands and completes the network in 609, joining the fertile south to his capital at Luoyang and to his armies on the northern frontier. Its present main stem is thought to run for 1,776 km, and it is a World Heritage Site.

label: The Tang dynasty
summary: Tang emperors govern China and reach into Central Asia. Chang’an, the capital, is among the largest cities in the world, and Buddhists, Daoists, Christians of the Church of the East, Manichaeans and Muslims all have a presence there.

label: The Hijra gives the Islamic calendar its starting point
summary: The Hijra, the journey of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina, gives the Hijri calendar its epoch: 1 Muharram, the first day of the year of the Hijra, equates to 16 July 622 in the Julian calendar. It is reported that Caliph Umar, about 638 (17 AH), after an official in Basra complained that Umar’s letters carried no years, designated the year of the Hijra as the first year of the Islamic calendar.

label: Rules for calculating with zero are written down in India
summary: The mathematician Brahmagupta, in a work finished in 628 CE, states rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero as a number. A dot used as a zero sign appears in the Bakhshali manuscript, long cited as the earliest Indian example, but radiocarbon tests have given dates from the 3rd to the 12th century CE for its leaves, and its age is disputed.

label: The Umayyad Caliphate rules from Damascus
summary: Mu’awiya, long the governor of Syria, becomes caliph in 661 after the First Fitna and founds hereditary rule by the Umayyad family, the second Islamic caliphate, with Damascus as its capital. Its territory is estimated at 11 to 15 million square kilometres; revolts and tribal rivalries weaken it, and it ends in 750.

label: Srivijaya, a Malay Buddhist sea power based on Sumatra
summary: Srivijaya, a Malay Buddhist thalassocracy based on Sumatra, is named in a 7th-century inscription found near Palembang, dated 16 June 682, and is an important centre for the spread of Buddhism from the 7th to the 11th century. It may have disintegrated after 1025, following several major raids by the Chola Empire on its ports. It was largely forgotten until modern scholars reconstructed its history.

label: The Dome of the Rock is built in Jerusalem
summary: The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik orders the building of an octagonal shrine over the Foundation Stone in Jerusalem, completed in 691–692; its inscription gives the date 72 AH. It is described as the oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture and carries early inscriptions proclaiming Islam and the prophet Muhammad. Accounts of when work began differ: 685/6 in one, 688 in another.

label: The Kanem–Bornu Empire rules around Lake Chad
summary: The Kanem–Bornu Empire, based around Lake Chad and sustained by the trans-Saharan trade, is believed to have been founded about 700, though later and earlier dates have been proposed; its early history is poorly known and the date is uncertain. The Duguwa dynasty rules from Njimi; in the 11th century the empire converts to Islam and the Sayfawa dynasty replaces the Duguwa, and it reaches its zenith in the 13th century under Dunama II Dibalemi. It is conquered in 1893.

summary: Two memorial steles are raised by the Göktürks in the Orkhon Valley in the early 8th century for the princes Kul Tigin and Bilge Qaghan, with texts in Middle Chinese and in Old Turkic written in the Old Turkic alphabet. They are the oldest preserved form of a Turkic language; the Danish philologist Vilhelm Thomsen deciphered them in 1893.

label: Camel caravans link the Sahel to the Mediterranean world
summary: Camel caravans carry salt, gold, ivory, cloth, metal goods and enslaved people across the Sahara between North Africa and the Sahel. The earliest evidence of domesticated camels in the region dates from the 3rd century CE; regular routes develop with the spread of Islam in West Africa in the 7th and 8th centuries, and the trade peaks from the 8th century to the early 17th.

label: The Abbasid caliphate; Baghdad is founded
summary: The Abbasid family takes the caliphate from the Umayyads in 750 and founds Baghdad as its capital in 762. Scholars there and elsewhere translate Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Abbasid rule in Baghdad ends when the Mongols take the city in 1258; a line of Abbasid caliphs without political power continues in Cairo until 1517.

label: Scholars in Baghdad translate Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic
summary: Under the Abbasid caliphs, with support from the court and wealthy patrons, scholars of several faiths translate Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit works on medicine, astronomy, mathematics and philosophy into Arabic and add work of their own. The “House of Wisdom” in Baghdad, linked with the caliph al-Ma’mun (813 to 833), is the best-known name; historians debate whether it was a centre of translation or mainly a library.

label: Borobudur, a Mahayana Buddhist temple, is built in central Java
summary: Borobudur, a Mahayana Buddhist temple of nine stacked platforms in central Java, has 2,672 relief panels and originally had 504 Buddha statues. Its date is given variously as the 8th century, in stages from about 780 under the Sailendra, and the 9th century. It was abandoned after the decline of Hindu kingdoms in Java in the 14th century, and UNESCO has listed it since 1991.

label: The Viking Age: raids, trade and settlement across the North Atlantic
summary: From the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, Scandinavian seafarers raid, trade and settle from the British Isles to Russia and cross the North Atlantic to Iceland, Greenland and, in the early 11th century, a short-lived camp in Newfoundland. The period is conventionally ended in 1066.

label: Charlemagne is crowned emperor in Rome
summary: Charlemagne, King of the Franks from 768 and King of the Lombards from 774, is crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III in 800, though historians debate the coronation. He unites most of Western and Central Europe, and is the first recognised emperor to rule from the west after the fall of the Western Roman Empire about three centuries earlier. His state is known as the Carolingian Empire.

label: The Classic Maya collapse
summary: Many cities of the southern Maya lowlands stop recording dates and are abandoned over about a century, while northern cities such as Chichén Itzá flourish. Drought, warfare, shifting trade routes and over-use of land have all been proposed, often in combination; scholars do not agree on the weight of each.

It is first named in a text of about 830 and becomes a vassal of Mali in the 13th century. Historians disagree about when it began, why it declined and whether its capital was Koumbi Saleh, an identification now disputed.

label: The Igbo-Ukwu bronzes: lost-wax casting, first dated to the 9th century
summary: Excavations at three sites at Igbo-Ukwu in south-eastern Nigeria have found bronze artifacts of a highly sophisticated metal-working culture, made by lost-wax casting. Thurstan Shaw’s radiocarbon dates put them in the 9th century CE, the date still commonly cited, but the calibrated range is the 7th to 12th centuries and an AMS date on a textile from one deposit gives the 11th or 12th. A villager, Isaiah Anozie, found the first works in 1938; Shaw excavated the sites from 1959.

label: The Khmer Empire rules mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor
summary: The beginning of the Khmer Empire is conventionally dated to 802, when the prince Jayavarman II declared himself chakravartin, a universal ruler. Centred on hydraulic cities in northern Cambodia, it rules or vassalises most of mainland Southeast Asia, and its end is traditionally marked by the fall of Angkor to the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1431. Scholars still debate the reasons for its collapse.

label: Al-Khwarizmi writes on algebra and on calculation with Hindu numerals

His work On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals, written about 825, was principally responsible for spreading the Hindu–Arabic numeral system; its Latin translation of the 12th century gave the word “algorithm” from his name.

The earliest datable mentions of the Cholas are in inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE, from the reign of Ashoka. In the 11th century Chola armies invade Sri Lanka, the Maldives and parts of Southeast Asia.

summary: Between about 900 and 1150, Chaco Canyon in what is now New Mexico is a major cultural centre for the Ancestral Puebloans, who quarry sandstone and haul timber from great distances to build 15 major complexes. Climate change is thought to have led to their eventual abandonment of the canyon, which began about 1140, perhaps triggered by an extreme 50-year drought from 1130.

A labourer unearthed it in 1987 during dredging near the mouth of the Lumbang River; it is written mainly in Old Malay in the Old Javanese Kawi script, with several technical Sanskrit terms.

summary: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting, writes a long prose tale of court life in the early 11th century that is often called the first novel. Buddhist ideas of impermanence run through it.

label: Ibn al-Haytham writes the Book of Optics

label: The Jalali solar calendar is adopted under the Seljuks

label: Great Zimbabwe, a stone-walled city of the southern African plateau
summary: A large town of dry-stone walls grows on the plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, linked by trade in gold and ivory to the Swahili coast. Early European writers assigned its building to outsiders; archaeology shows it was built by the ancestors of Shona-speaking people.

label: Angkor Wat is built
summary: King Suryavarman II has a very large temple to the god Vishnu built at his capital. Khmer kings had favoured Shiva and Vishnu; the temple later becomes a Buddhist site and is still in use today.

label: Scholars at Toledo translate Arabic science and philosophy into Latin
summary: After Christian forces take Toledo in 1085 and inherit its libraries, a group of scholars translates Islamic philosophical and scientific works from Arabic into medieval Latin in the 12th and 13th centuries. The first period is led by Raymond, archbishop of Toledo from 1126 to 1151; under Alfonso X of Castile in the 13th century the translators no longer used Latin as the final language.

label: The Almohads rule the Maghreb and al-Andalus
summary: The Almohad movement of the Masmuda Berbers, inspired by Ibn Tumart and based at Tinmel in the Atlas Mountains, overthrows the Almoravids and captures Marrakesh in 1147; its caliph Abd al-Mu’min reigns from 1130 to 1163. The Almohad empire rules much of the Maghreb and al-Andalus until 1269, and its power in Iberia turns after the caliph Muhammad al-Nasir’s defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

label: Zhu Xi shapes Neo-Confucianism
summary: Zhu Xi (1130–1200), a philosopher, historian and politician of the Southern Song, is a leading figure in the development of Neo-Confucianism and tries to integrate moral self-cultivation, classical interpretation, ritual practice and cosmological theory. His commentaries on the Four Books become the core texts of the imperial civil service examinations from 1313, and his doctrines are taken up in Japan, Korea and Vietnam.

label: Al-Idrisi completes the Tabula Rogeriana for Roger II of Sicily
summary: The Norman king Roger II commissions an atlas in 1138 and the Moroccan geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi, invited to his court in Palermo, completes it in 1154, a few weeks before the king’s death. The Nuzhat al-mushtāq, known in the West as the Tabula Rogeriana, compiles 70 maps of the known world with commentary on each place; the maps are oriented with north at the bottom, south at the top and Mecca in the middle.

The date is not agreed: reference works give about 1102, 1142 (read from a solar eclipse) or 1190, many archaeologists and anthropologists favour about 1450, and one says likely between 1142 and 1660. The Tuscarora join in 1722.

label: The Hanseatic League links the towns of the North Sea and the Baltic
summary: The Hanseatic League, a medieval commercial and defensive network of merchant guilds and market towns, grows from Lübeck and a few other North German towns in the late 12th century and by the 15th encompasses nearly 200 settlements in eight modern countries, from Estonia and Russia to the Netherlands. It has trading posts (Kontors) in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod, and it disintegrates in 1669.

summary: The Edo kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, grows out of the older Igodomigodo, and its line of obas is traced by tradition to about 1180. In the 15th and 16th centuries it expands, trades with Portugal and other European states and produces cast bronzes, ironwork and carved ivory. Britain annexes it in 1897; the monarchy continues without sovereignty.

label: Nan Madol, a city of stone islands, is built on Pohnpei
summary: Megalithic construction at Nan Madol, a city of small artificial islands linked by canals on a lagoon off Pohnpei, begins about 1180–1200, with large basalt stones taken from a volcanic plug on the other side of the island. By Pohnpeian tradition it is the capital of the Saudeleur dynasty until about 1628, when Isokelekel overthrows the Saudeleurs; his successors later abandon the site.

label: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela
summary: Lalibela, in the Lasta district of Ethiopia, has rock-cut monolithic churches. Their dating is uncertain: they are traditionally attributed to the reign of the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela (r. about 1181–1221), but the page says it is more likely that they reached their present form over several phases of construction and alteration, and dates the churches from the 7th to the 13th century. They were declared a World Heritage Site in 1978.

label: The moai of Rapa Nui, and the explanations of the island’s depopulation
summary: The Rapa Nui people, who settled the island about 1200 CE, create nearly 1,000 monumental statues, the moai; UNESCO listed the island in 1995. Explanations of its depopulation differ: Jared Diamond proposed that deforestation, helped by the introduced Polynesian rat, led to a collapse before Europeans arrived in 1722, while a 2021 study finds steady growth until then; others stress European diseases, Peruvian slave raids and emigration, and between 1862 and 1888 about 94% of the population perished or emigrated.

label: The Delhi Sultanate rules much of the subcontinent
summary: The sultanate is established in 1206 in former Ghurid territory and is generally divided into five periods: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. Timur’s raid on Delhi in 1398 coincides with the rise of rival powers such as Vijayanagara and the Bahmani sultanate. In 1526 Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi, the last sultan, and the Mughal Empire replaces it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Delhi Sultanate
sources.note: read: the five periods, the raid of 1398, the end in 1526

label: The Mongol Empire
summary: Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206. He and his successors build the largest land empire in history, from the Sea of Japan to eastern Europe, joining trade routes across Eurasia; it divides into separate khanates, and the Yuan dynasty in China ends in 1368. Estimates of the numbers killed in the conquests vary widely among historians.

related.note: The plague reached the Black Sea ports by routes that Mongol rule had joined; historians differ on how far that explains its spread.

label: Magna Carta
summary: King John of England, pressed by his barons, seals a charter in June 1215 that limits some royal powers and promises that free men will not be punished except by lawful judgment. Its first clause guarantees the freedom of the English church. It is reissued many times and later cited in arguments about law and liberty.

label: The Mali Empire: gold, salt and learning in West Africa
summary: From Sundiata’s victory about 1235, Mali grows into a large state controlling gold and salt routes across the Sahara. Its ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324. The early history rests on oral tradition and later Arabic accounts.

label: The Epic of Sundiata tells of the founding of the Mali Empire
summary: The Epic of Sundiata, a poem of the Malinke people, tells how Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire and ruled from 1235 until his death in 1255. Griots have narrated it for generations through oral tradition, and its modern version rests on the oral account of the griot Djeli Mamoudou Kouyaté, translated into French. Oral tradition is one of the sources, with records such as Ibn Khaldun’s, for the history of the period.

label: The Mamluk Sultanate rules Egypt, the Levant and the Hejaz
summary: A military caste of mamluks, freed slave soldiers, headed by a sultan overthrows the Ayyubid dynasty in Egypt in 1250 and rules Egypt, the Levant and the Hejaz from Cairo until the Ottoman conquest of 1517. Its history is divided into the Bahri period (1250–1382) and the Burji period (1382–1517); in 1260 the Mamluks under Sultan Qutuz and Baybars rout the Mongols and halt their southward expansion.

label: The Samalas eruption of 1257 in Lombok
summary: A catastrophic eruption at Samalas on Lombok, of probable volcanic explosivity index 7, buries much of the island and destroys the city of Pamatan; ash falls 340 km away in Java. An ice-core sulfate spike from about 1257 had shown a large eruption, and in 2013 scientists linked it to records of Samalas on palm-leaf manuscripts. The eruption cooled the climate for several years; the scale of the cooling and its consequences, such as famine, are still debated.

label: The Maragheh observatory is built under Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
summary: Under the patronage of the Ilkhanid ruler Hulagu, the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi directs the building of an observatory at Maragheh in what is now East Azerbaijan, Iran, begun in 1259 and lasting between three and five years, with an integrated library. The page says that it was considered one of the most advanced scientific institutions in Eurasia.

label: Marco Polo travels through Asia and his book records it
summary: The Venetian merchant Marco Polo travels through Asia along the Silk Road between 1271 and 1295 and, by his book’s account, is received at the court of Kublai Khan. His account rests on what he dictated, about 1300, to Rustichello da Pisa, a fellow prisoner after the Genoese captured him in the war with Venice; his book, Il Milione, describes the culture and wealth of the East. Some have doubted that he reached China; others find his account of it more accurate and detailed than other travellers’.

label: The Timbuktu manuscripts: Arabic and African-language learning in the Sahel
summary: From the late 13th century to the early 20th, households in Timbuktu kept manuscripts in Arabic, and in Songhay, Fula, Tamasheq and other African languages written in Arabic script, on subjects including medicine, science and philosophy as well as copies of the Quran. Most remain uncatalogued, so any figure for their number is a rough estimate.

label: Majapahit, a Hindu-Buddhist sea empire based on Java
summary: Majapahit, a Javanese Hindu-Buddhist thalassocratic empire, begins with the settlement that Raden Wijaya founds in 1292 in the forest of Trik. The Nagarakṛtāgama, written in 1365, describes an empire of 98 tributaries. Dates for its end range from 1478 to 1527, the later after an invasion by the Sultanate of Demak, and Islamic kingdoms rise in Java.

label: The Ottoman beylik is founded in north-western Anatolia
summary: A principality is founded in north-western Anatolia about 1299 by the Turkoman leader Osman I, as the Rum Sultanate declines and Anatolia is a patchwork of independent Turkish states; sources for these years are scarce, so the date is approximate, and a Byzantine defeat at Bapheus in 1302 contributed to his rise. His successors conquer much of Anatolia and expand into the Balkans by the mid-14th century.

label: The Little Ice Age, a period of regional cooling
summary: The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, particularly pronounced in the North Atlantic region, and not a true ice age of global extent. It is conventionally defined as running from the 16th to the 19th century, but definitions differ, and some experts prefer about 1300 to about 1850; NASA’s Earth Observatory notes three especially cold intervals, beginning about 1650, 1770 and 1850. Several causes have been proposed, among them cyclical lows in solar radiation and heightened volcanic activity.

label: Dante writes the Divine Comedy
summary: The Florentine poet Dante Alighieri, in exile from his city, writes a long poem in Italian about a journey through hell, purgatory and heaven. It draws on classical and medieval learning, and its images shape later European art and writing.

label: The Great Famine of 1315–1317 strikes most of Europe

places.name: Northern Europe (from Poland to the Alps)

summary: The Great Famine of 1315–1317, occasionally dated 1315–1322, is the first of a series of large-scale crises in early 14th-century Europe, affecting most of Europe from Poland to the Alps. It starts with bad weather in spring 1315 and crop failures that last through 1316 until the summer harvest of 1317, and causes widespread population loss over an extended number of years, ending the growth and prosperity of the 11th to 13th centuries.

summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, travels to Mecca in 1324–1325 by way of Cairo with a large retinue and much gold. The Arab writer al-Umari, who visited Cairo some years later, was told that the gold spent there kept its price low for about twelve years. Later Arabic accounts give widely varying figures for his caravan, and modern historians treat those figures as rhetorical rather than exact.

label: Ibn Battuta travels through Africa, Asia and Iberia
summary: Ibn Battuta, a Muslim scholar from Tangier, travels over thirty years, from 1325 to 1354, visiting much of Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula. Near the end of his life he dictates an account of his journeys, A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling, known as the Rihla; scholars doubt that he made some of the journeys it describes, such as a trip up the Volga to Bolghar.

label: The Vijayanagara Empire rules much of southern India from Hampi
summary: The brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I found the empire in 1336, after the Delhi Sultanate’s incursions into the Deccan; at its peak under Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529) it holds much of the peninsula. Its central authority diminishes sharply after defeat by allied Deccan sultanates at Talikota in 1565, and it survives until 1646. The ruins of its capital near Hampi are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

label: The Black Death
summary: Plague reaches the Black Sea ports in 1346 and spreads across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East by 1353, along trade routes. Estimates of the share of Europe’s people who died range from about a quarter to 60 percent. People fled, imposed quarantines and held processions, and Jewish communities and other minorities were attacked after being blamed for the disease.

related.note: Both were caused by the same bacterium, Yersinia pestis.

label: The Ayutthaya Kingdom rules the Chao Phraya basin
summary: The Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya exists from 1351 to 1767. European travellers of the early 16th century name it, with Vijayanagara and Ming China, as one of the three great powers of Asia. Burmese Konbaung armies invade in 1759–1760 and 1765–1767, and the city falls in April 1767 after a siege of fourteen months.
