label: The Ming dynasty rules China
summary: The Ming dynasty rules China from 1368 to 1644, after the collapse of the Mongol-led Yuan, and is the last imperial dynasty ruled by the Han people. The Hongwu Emperor (r. 1368–1398) tries to create a society of self-sufficient rural communities; under the Yongle Emperor, from 1402, Beijing becomes a capital. The eunuch Zheng He leads seven voyages into the Indian Ocean, and the Great Wall is fortified into its modern form; rump regimes of the Ming family last until 1662.

label: Timur founds the Timurid Empire
summary: Timur (Tamerlane), a Barlas warlord, founds the Timurid Empire, a Turco-Mongol, Persianate and Muslim empire, ruling from 1370 to 1405 from Samarkand and dominating Greater Iran in the early 15th century. Its Timurid Renaissance flourishes particularly under Shah Rukh and under his astronomer and mathematician son Ulugh Beg (1447–1449); by 1507 the Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan have conquered almost all of the surviving Timurid lands.

summary: The Jikji, an anthology of Buddhist Zen teachings, is printed in July 1377 at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju during the Goryeo dynasty. UNESCO confirmed it in 2001 as the oldest extant book printed with movable metal type and inscribed it on its Memory of the World Register. It was printed 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible.

summary: A kingdom in west-central Africa, in what is now northern Angola and the western Congo region, is an independent state from about 1390 to 1862; its early history comes from oral traditions first written down in the late 16th century. A Portuguese expedition reaches its coast in 1483; its king Nzinga a Nkuwu is baptised in 1491, and after Afonso I wins a contest for the throne in 1509, Catholicism becomes the religion of the ruling court. From 1862 to 1914 it is, intermittently, a vassal of Portugal.

summary: The conventional thesis dates the Malacca Sultanate to about 1400, founded by Parameswara, formerly king of Singapura, though earlier dates have been proposed. In the 15th century its capital grows into one of the most important transshipment ports of its time and a centre of Islamic learning and of the Malay language. It falls to the Portuguese in 1511.

label: The Renaissance in Italy and beyond
summary: Scholars, artists and patrons in Florence, Rome, Venice and elsewhere study and imitate Greek and Roman models and develop new methods in painting, architecture and writing. Historians still debate when it began and how sharply the period differs from the Middle Ages.

label: Zheng He’s fleets sail from China to India, Arabia and East Africa
summary: Seven voyages led by the court official Zheng He cross the Indian Ocean with large fleets, bringing gifts to rulers and receiving embassies in return. The Ming court then ends the voyages.

related.note: Chinese fleets crossed the Indian Ocean some ninety years before the Portuguese arrived.

label: The Forbidden City is built in Beijing
summary: Construction of the Forbidden City begins in 1406, when the capital is moved from Nanjing to Beijing, and lasts 14 years, needing more than a million workers. It is the seat of the Ming dynasty from 1420 to 1644 and the residence of twenty-four Ming and Qing emperors, the centre of political power in China until 1924; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

label: Machu Picchu is built as an Inca estate
summary: The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, on a mountain ridge in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru, is estimated to have been built about 1450 and is believed to have served as an estate for the emperor Pachacuti, though no contemporary written records exist. Modern radiocarbon dating places its occupation between about 1420 and 1530; it was abandoned about a century later, and Hiram Bingham III brought it to international attention in 1911. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1983.

label: The Aztec Triple Alliance
summary: The cities of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan join to defeat a rival power and then collect tribute across central Mexico. Our knowledge of the founding comes mostly from accounts written after the Spanish conquest.

label: The Inca Empire
summary: Under Pachacuti and his successors the Inca state grows from the Cusco valley to run along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile, held together by roads and a system of labour service. The Incas had no writing, and the early dates rest on accounts set down after the Spanish conquest.

label: King Sejong’s court creates the Korean alphabet, Hangul
summary: King Sejong of Joseon (r. 1418–1450) moves to create a writing system for Korean, which had been written with Chinese characters. The script is announced in late 1443 or early 1444 and officially published in 1446 in the Hunminjeongeum and its commentary, the Hunminjeongeum Haerye.

summary: Johannes Gutenberg’s workshop develops a way of casting metal type and printing with a press; the 42-line Bible of about 1455 is the first major book printed this way in Europe. Movable type had been used earlier in China and Korea.

label: The Ottomans take Constantinople
summary: After a siege of about seven weeks, Ottoman forces under Mehmed II enter Constantinople on 29 May 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire. The city becomes the Ottoman capital.

label: The Songhai state rules the Niger bend from Gao
summary: Under Sonni Ali (from about 1464) and then the Askia dynasty (1493 to 1591), the Songhai state, centred on Gao, takes Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné in 1475. Leo Africanus, who visited Timbuktu in the early 1500s, wrote of its mosque, its cloth trade and the books brought from North Africa that sold for more than any other goods. The state ends after an invasion from Morocco in 1591.

summary: After Columbus’s first voyage, crops such as maize, potatoes and tomatoes, animals such as horses and cattle, and diseases move between the Americas and the rest of the world, changing diets, populations and landscapes on both sides.

label: Portugal and Castile divide the world outside Europe at Tordesillas
summary: The Treaty of Tordesillas, signed on 7 June 1494 and ratified at Setúbal, divides the newly discovered lands outside Europe between the Kingdom of Portugal and the Crown of Castile along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. It replaces a line drawn by Pope Alexander VI’s bull Inter caetera 100 leagues west; the other side of the world was divided later, by the Treaty of Zaragoza of 22 April 1529.

summary: A Portuguese fleet reaches Calicut in May 1498 after rounding the Cape of Good Hope, opening a direct sea route between Europe and the Indian Ocean trade, which had long been carried by others.

label: The transatlantic slave trade
summary: Ships from Europe and the Americas carry millions of enslaved Africans to the Americas, where they are forced to work, mostly on plantations. summary: Shah Ismail I founds the Safavid dynasty in 1501; it rules Iran until 1736, though some historians date its fall to 1722, when Isfahan fell to the Afghans. It establishes Twelver Shi’ism as the state religion of Iran and spreads Shia Islam in major parts of Central Asia, the Caucasus and Anatolia. label: Epidemics in the Americas after 1492
summary: Smallpox, measles and other diseases from Europe and Africa reach people with no earlier exposure; smallpox is first recorded in the Americas in 1518, and the first great epidemic reaches Mexico in 1520. The losses were severe, and disease and the conditions of colonial rule both played a part; estimates of the populations before and after contact differ widely.

summary: A Spanish expedition planned and first led by the Portuguese Ferdinand Magellan, to secure a sea route to the Moluccas, leaves Spain on 20 September 1519 with five ships and about 270 men, enters the strait that bears his name on 1 November 1520 and reaches the Moluccas in November 1521. label: Babur founds the Mughal Empire
summary: Babur, a ruler from Central Asia, defeats the sultan of Delhi at Panipat on 21 April 1526. The dynasty he founds rules most of the subcontinent into the 18th century, and nominally until 1857.

label: The Scientific Revolution: from Copernicus to Newton
summary: Copernicus’s sun-centred model is printed in 1543; Galileo’s telescope observations follow in 1609 to 1610, Kepler’s laws, and Newton’s Principia in 1687. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition found Galileo “vehemently suspect of heresy” for defending the sun-centred model. Historians still debate how sudden or unified the change was.

label: The cocoliztli epidemics devastate New Spain
summary: An illness with high fevers and bleeding, which the Aztecs called cocoliztli, “pestilence”, causes an estimated 5 to 15 million deaths in New Spain in the 16th century, with the largest outbreaks in 1545 and 1576. Its cause is debated: genomic studies suggest that Salmonella enterica serotype Paratyphi C was at least partly responsible, while others think it was an indigenous viral haemorrhagic fever, perhaps made worse by severe drought.

label: The silver of Potosí begins to flow
summary: The indigenous prospector Diego Huallpa is traditionally credited with discovering the silver of the Cerro Rico at Potosí in 1545; the town founded that year soon produces great wealth, and its population probably exceeds 100,000 by 1600 and, on the Wikipedia page’s account, eventually exceeds 200,000. Native Andeans are made to work in the mines through the Spanish mita system of forced labour, which is based on a pre-Hispanic Andean practice of the same name.

label: The Popol Vuh of the Kʼicheʼ Maya is recorded in writing
summary: The Popol Vuh, a foundational narrative of the Kʼicheʼ people of Guatemala recounting their mythology and history, is preserved by oral tradition until about 1550, when it is recorded in writing. The text that survives is credited to the Dominican friar Francisco Ximénez, who in 1701 came to Chichicastenango and prepared a manuscript with the Kʼicheʼ text and a Spanish translation in parallel columns.

label: The Shaanxi earthquake of 1556
summary: One of the deadliest earthquakes in history strikes Huaxian in Shaanxi in the early morning of 23 January 1556, under the Ming dynasty. Most residents lived in yaodongs, artificial caves in loess cliffs, which collapsed and buried people as they slept. Modern estimates of the China Earthquake Administration put the direct deaths at roughly 100,000, with over 700,000 more who migrated away or died of famine and plagues, a total reduction of 830,000 in the imperial household registers.

summary: The Manila galleon trade route, in use from 1565 to 1815, links the Philippines in the Spanish East Indies to Mexico across the Pacific, with one or two round-trip voyages a year between Manila and Acapulco. It is inaugurated in 1565 after the Augustinian friar Andrés de Urdaneta pioneers the return route east, taking advantage of the Kuroshio current.

label: Russia extends its rule across Siberia
summary: The Russian conquest of Siberia takes place between 1581 and 1778, when the Khanate of Sibir, a loose structure of vassalages, is undermined by Russian explorers. It is traditionally considered to begin in July 1581, when some 540 Cossacks under Yermak Timofeyevich invade the lands of the Voguls. Though outnumbered, the Russians press the tribes into changing their loyalties and set up distant forts from which they raid.

label: Pope Gregory XIII replaces the Julian calendar
summary: The papal bull Inter gravissimas, issued by Pope Gregory XIII, replaces the Julian calendar by one whose leap years are spaced to give a mean year of 365.2425 days; in October 1582 Thursday 4 October is followed by Friday 15 October. Other countries follow later: Britain and its colonies in September 1752, and the last European country to adopt it did so in 1923, for civil use only. Many Orthodox churches still use the Julian calendar for the dating of major feasts.

label: The English East India Company is founded
summary: The East India Company, an English and later British joint-stock company, is founded in 1600 for Indian Ocean trade, at first with the East Indies and later with East Asia. Its rule in the Indian subcontinent expands after the Battle of Plassey in 1757, and by 1858 it controls most of modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh; after the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act 1858 has the Crown assume direct control, and the company is dissolved in 1874.

summary: The States General of the Netherlands grant the United East India Company a 21-year monopoly of trade in Asia on 20 March 1602, by joining existing companies; it is one of the first joint-stock companies, and its shares trade on open-air markets, one of which becomes the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. The company has quasi-governmental powers, including waging war. It is dissolved on 31 December 1799, its possessions and debts taken over by the state.

summary: After victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu becomes shogun in 1603 and the Tokugawa clan governs Japan from Edo Castle with the daimyō lords until 1868, ending the civil wars of the Sengoku period. In the 1630s the shogunate adopts the policies called sakoku, which bar the entry of most foreigners and Japanese subjects from leaving.

label: Galileo publishes the Sidereus Nuncius
summary: Galileo Galilei publishes the Sidereus Nuncius, the “Starry Messenger”, a short treatise in Latin, on 13 March 1610. The page calls it the first published scientific work based on observations made through a telescope; it reports a Moon with mountains and imperfections, hundreds of stars not visible to the naked eye in the Milky Way and in constellations, and four Medicean Stars, the moons of Jupiter.

label: The Thirty Years’ War
summary: A revolt in Bohemia in 1618 grows into a war that draws in most of Europe’s states and is fought mostly across the German lands. It ends with the Peace of Westphalia. Armies, hunger and disease caused heavy losses of life, and some regions lost a large part of their people.

summary: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissions the Taj Mahal in 1631 to house the tomb of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and his own. The marble mausoleum is completed in 1648 and the rest of the complex by 1653, at a cost estimated at the time at about ₹32 million, with more than 20,000 workers and artisans under a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori.

label: Rangaku, Dutch learning, keeps Japan in touch with Western science
summary: Rangaku, “Dutch learning”, and by extension Yōgaku, “Western learning”, is the body of knowledge that Japan develops through its contacts with the Dutch enclave at Dejima, which lets it keep abreast of Western technology and medicine while the country is closed to foreigners, from 1641 to 1853, under the Tokugawa shogunate’s policy of national seclusion.

label: The Manchu-led Qing dynasty takes Beijing
summary: A Manchu-led dynasty, which had risen from the Later Jin state, seizes the Ming capital Beijing in 1644, traditionally taken as the start of Qing rule (some reckon the dynasty from 1636). It lasts until the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 and the abdication of the last emperor in 1912. At its height the empire stretched from the Sea of Japan to the Pamir Mountains and from the Mongolian Plateau to the South China Sea.

label: The Peace of Westphalia
summary: Treaties signed in two Westphalian cities end the Thirty Years’ War. They confirm that each German ruler may choose Catholic, Lutheran or Reformed worship for their lands, and are often cited as an early step toward a system of sovereign states.

label: Shivaji is crowned and the Maratha state grows into an empire
summary: The Marathas, a Marathi-speaking warrior group from the western Deccan, rise under Shivaji, crowned Chhatrapati of the new Maratha Kingdom in 1674 after he fought the Mughals. The empire, a confederacy of the Peshwa’s realm and four major Maratha states, has its expansion halted by the defeat at Panipat in 1761, and the East India Company’s intervention in the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha Wars destroys the confederacy by 1818.

label: The Enlightenment
summary: Writers and scientists in Britain, France, Germany, Scotland and the Americas argue for reason, evidence and toleration as guides in religion, politics and knowledge. They include believers, sceptics and deists; the Encyclopédie (1751 to 1772) is among its monuments. Dates for the period vary by author.

related.note: Historians debate how far.

label: The Asante Kingdom conquers Denkyira and grows into an empire
summary: The Asante Empire, an Akan state in what is now Ghana, lasts from 1701 to 1902. In the late 17th century the king Osei Tutu and his adviser Okomfo Anokye found the Asante Kingdom with the Golden Stool as its sole unifying symbol; in 1701 the Asante army conquers Denkyira, which gives access to the Gulf of Guinea, and the empire expands to include most of Ghana and parts of Ivory Coast and Togo.

label: İbrahim Müteferrika runs the first Muslim-run press with movable Arabic type
summary: İbrahim Müteferrika, a Hungarian-born Ottoman diplomat and the first Muslim to run a printing press with movable Arabic type, receives permission from Sultan Ahmed III to publish non-religious books, despite opposition from some religious leaders. His press publishes its first book in 1729 and by 1743 has issued 17 works in 23 volumes; an earlier Ottoman press with movable Arabic type, run by Christians in Aleppo, had worked in 1706–1711.

label: Jai Singh completes the Jantar Mantar observatory at Jaipur
summary: Sawai Jai Singh, the Rajput king who founded Jaipur, completes the Jantar Mantar in 1734, a collection of 19 astronomical instruments that allow the observation of astronomical positions with the naked eye; its Vrihat Samrat Yantra is described as the world’s largest gnomon sundial. The observatory is an example of Ptolemaic positional astronomy and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

label: Macassan trepangers begin to visit northern Australia
summary: Makassarese merchants and Sama-Bajau fishermen from southern Sulawesi begin to visit the coast of northern Australia about the middle of the 18th century, first in the Kimberley and some decades later in Arnhem Land, to collect and process trepang, the sea cucumber prized in Chinese markets; earlier starts are argued, about 1720 and the mid-1600s or earlier from rock art. The Makassar word for it, taripaŋ, enters the Aboriginal languages of the Cobourg Peninsula as tharriba.

label: The Lisbon earthquake
summary: On All Saints’ Day, 1 November 1755, an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroy much of Lisbon; deaths are estimated in the tens of thousands. Writers across Europe, including Voltaire and Rousseau, argue about what it shows of nature and providence.

related.note: Voltaire and others answered it in print.

label: The Industrial Revolution begins in Britain
summary: Coal-fired steam engines (Newcomen’s in 1712, Watt’s improved engine from the 1770s), machine spinning of cotton and cheap iron reshape work and cities in Britain and then elsewhere. Historians debate when it began and how sudden it was.

label: James Cook leads three voyages of exploration to the Pacific
summary: Captain James Cook, a Royal Navy officer, leads three voyages of exploration to the Pacific and Southern Oceans between 1768 and 1779. The stated aim of the first is to observe the transit of Venus of 1769 from Tahiti; he makes the first recorded circumnavigation of the main islands of New Zealand and leads the first recorded European visits to the east coast of Australia and to the Hawaiian Islands. He is killed in Hawaiʻi in 1779 when a dispute with Native Hawaiians turns violent.

label: The Great Bengal famine of 1769–1770
summary: A famine in Bengal and Bihar in 1769–1770 affects some 30 million people, about a third of the population, during a period of dual governance: the East India Company holds the diwani, the right to collect revenue, while the Nawab of Bengal keeps the civil administration. Estimates of the dead differ: seven to ten million were thought to have died, but later demographic estimates, made where figures were lacking in 1770, are lower, at least one million.

label: Tupaia draws a chart of the Pacific for Cook
summary: The Polynesian navigator and priest Tupaia of Raʻiātea joins Cook’s Endeavour as guide, and on 15 August 1769 begins a Chart of the Pacific Ocean with Cook, Banks and Cook’s officers. He draws all 130 islands within some 2,000 miles and names 74; recent research finds that his chart shows voyaging routes from Rotuma to Rapa Nui and that his knowledge reached throughout the Polynesian triangle, a view that differs from older work that took his own voyaging to be limited.

summary: On 2 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress votes for independence, twelve colonies in favour and New York abstaining, and on 4 July, meeting in the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia, approves the Declaration, which says the colonies “are, and of Right ought to be Free and Independent States”. The engrossed copy is titled “The unanimous declaration” by a resolution of 19 July. Jefferson wrote the first draft for a Committee of Five appointed on 11 June; Congress edited it.

label: The First Fleet reaches Botany Bay and the colony is settled at Sydney Cove
summary: Eleven British ships carrying convicts, marines and officials under Captain Arthur Phillip leave Portsmouth on 13 May 1787 and reach Botany Bay on 18 January 1788; Phillip rejects it and chooses Port Jackson, and about 1,373 people are believed to have landed at Sydney Cove. This begins the British colonisation of Australia; the fleet meets the Eora people of the Sydney area, among them the Cadigal.

label: The French Revolution
summary: A crisis of royal finances leads to the meeting of the Estates General in 1789, the end of the monarchy in 1792, a republic, a period of mass violence, and finally Napoleon’s seizure of power in 1799. It changes the relation of church and state in France.

label: Smallpox devastates the Aboriginal people of Sydney in 1789
summary: A smallpox outbreak in 1789 devastates the Aboriginal people near the Sydney colony, killing perhaps half of them while sparing the British. Debate among modern medical and historical experts about the identity of the disease, how it reached Australia and why it did not infect the British is ongoing; some argue that the main agent of death was chickenpox, to which the British were largely immune.

label: Kamehameha unites the Hawaiian islands
summary: In 1795 Kamehameha sets sail with an armada of 960 war canoes and 10,000 soldiers and quickly secures the lightly defended islands, beginning with Maui, then conquers Oʻahu later that year. Kauaʻi, the last island outside his control, joins in April 1810, when he negotiates its peaceful unification with its ruler, Kaumualiʻi, and the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi is united.

label: Edward Jenner publishes his smallpox vaccination trials
summary: Jenner, an English country doctor, inoculates a boy with cowpox in 1796 and shows that he resists smallpox, and publishes the results in 1798. Vaccination spreads across the world, and in 1980 the World Health Organization declares smallpox eradicated.

label: The Rosetta Stone is found, and Champollion announces the reading of hieroglyphs
summary: A stele inscribed with a decree of 196 BCE for Ptolemy V in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, with only minor differences between the three, is found at Rosetta in July 1799 by a French officer, Pierre-François Bouchard, during France’s invasion of Egypt. The first complete translation of the Greek text is published in 1803, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion announces in Paris the transliteration of the Egyptian scripts.

label: The United States buys Louisiana from France

summary: In 1803 the United States buys Louisiana from France for $15 million, nominally some 828,000 square miles of the Mississippi basin west of the river. France controlled only a small part of it and most was inhabited by Native Americans, so the United States chiefly bought the preemptive right to obtain Indian lands by treaty or conquest. Napoleon sold after failing to suppress the revolt in Saint-Domingue and facing renewed war with the United Kingdom; Jefferson was eager to gain New Orleans.

label: Haiti declares its independence
summary: On 1 January 1804, from the city of Gonaïves, Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares the independence of the former French colony of Saint-Domingue, renaming it Haiti after the indigenous Arawak name. It follows the revolution of the enslaved that began in 1791; the page describes it as one of the only known slave rebellions that led to a state both free from slavery, though not from forced labour, and ruled by formerly enslaved people.

label: The Napoleonic Code is established in France
summary: The French civil code, the Napoleonic Code, is established during the Consulate in 1804, drafted by a commission of four jurists, and is still in force in France though much amended. It marks the abolition of the previous patchwork of feudal laws and, the page says, strongly influenced the law of many countries formed during and after the Napoleonic Wars, and of countries outside Europe, in the Middle East and in Latin America.

label: Usman dan Fodio founds the Sokoto Caliphate
summary: Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar, founds the Sokoto Caliphate in 1804 after defeating the Hausa kingdoms in the Fulani War. It extends over parts of what are now Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon and Burkina Faso, with a population estimated at 10 to 20 million by 1837. British, French and German forces end it as a state in 1903.

France abolishes slavery in its remaining colonies by a decree of 27 April 1848, the United States ends it after its Civil War, and slavery is abolished in Cuba in 1886 and in Brazil in 1888 by the Lei Áurea, when Brazil becomes the last country in the Americas to outlaw it.

label: Tambora erupts; 1816, the “year without a summer”
summary: The April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia is the largest in recorded history. Ash and gases cool the climate in 1816, with crop failures in Europe and North America and disrupted monsoons in Asia.

label: The first cholera pandemic spreads from Bengal
summary: Cholera, which had spread across India many times before, breaks out near Calcutta in 1817 and this time travels farther: through South and Southeast Asia to the Middle East, East Africa and the Mediterranean coast, as far as China and the Mediterranean Sea, before subsiding in 1824. Millions of people died, among them about 10,000 troops in British service, which drew the attention of Europe.

Portugal gives formal recognition in the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro of 29 August 1825, in exchange for compensation that Brazil agrees to pay. summary: On 29 August 1842 the British representative Sir Henry Pottinger and Qing representatives sign the Treaty of Nanjing, which ends the First Opium War, and it is ratified at Hong Kong on 26 June 1843. label: The Great Irish Famine
summary: A blight destroys the potato crops on which millions of people in Ireland depended. About a million people died and about a million more emigrated. Historians still debate how far the policies of the British government shaped the outcome.

label: The Taiping Rebellion
summary: Hong Xiuquan, who had come to believe he was the younger brother of Jesus, leads a movement that sets up the “Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace” at Nanjing and fights the Qing government for fourteen years. It ends with the fall of Nanjing in 1864; fighting, famine and disease caused very heavy loss of life. Some historians prefer the name Taiping Civil War.

summary: The United States and the Tokugawa shogunate sign the Convention of Kanagawa on 31 March 1854, under threat of force, after the expedition of Commodore Perry in 1853. It effectively ends Japan’s 220-year policy of national seclusion by opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American vessels, and it secures the safety of American sailors.

label: The third plague pandemic begins in Yunnan
summary: The third plague pandemic, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, begins in Yunnan in 1855 and spreads to all inhabited continents, ultimately causing at least 15 million deaths, among them 10 to 12 million in British India and 2.2 million in China. In Canton from March 1894 the disease killed 80,000 people in a few weeks. The World Health Organization considered the pandemic active until 1960, when deaths fell below 200 a year.

label: The germ theory of disease is established by Pasteur and Koch
summary: The germ theory, that microorganisms called pathogens cause infectious diseases, is the scientific theory now accepted to explain them. Its proof begins in the late 1850s with the work of Louis Pasteur and is extended by Robert Koch in the 1880s. Earlier practical work such as Ignaz Semmelweis’s at the Vienna General Hospital, which linked puerperal fever to examinations by doctors who had handled autopsies, made doctors wash their hands with chlorinated lime water.

label: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
summary: Charles Darwin’s book sets out evolution by natural selection, drawing on decades of observation; Alfred Russel Wallace had reached the same idea independently. Responses from scientists, churches and others range from acceptance to rejection, and discussion of how it relates to religion continues.

label: The Meiji Restoration
summary: In 1868 samurai leaders from several domains restore direct imperial rule in Japan and end the Tokugawa shogunate. The new government builds a modern army, schools and state, and gives Shinto shrines a new official role.

label: Mendeleev publishes his periodic table of the elements
summary: The periodic table that became generally accepted is that of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, who formulated the periodic law as a dependence of chemical properties on atomic mass. Since not all elements were then known, his table had gaps, and he successfully used the law to predict some properties of the missing elements. By 2010 the first 118 elements were known.

label: The Suez Canal opens between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea
summary: The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps forms the Compagnie de Suez in 1858, construction begins the next year, and the canal opens on 17 November 1869 as a single-lane waterway under French control. It links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea across the Isthmus of Suez, is 193.3 km long, and is a key trade route between Europe and Asia.

label: The Great Famine of 1876–1878 in India
summary: A famine begins in 1876 after an intense drought causes crop failure on the Deccan Plateau, spreads to Madras, Bombay, Mysore and Hyderabad and in 1877 to parts of northern India, and in the end affects an area of 670,000 square kilometres. The excess mortality is estimated in the range of 5.6 to 9.6 million. The colonial government continued to export grain during the famine, and its Bengal officials were criticised at the time for excessive spending on charitable relief.

label: The Northern Chinese famine of 1876–1879
summary: A famine marked by drought-induced crop failures and widespread starvation, known in Chinese as the Dingwu famine, kills between 9.5 and 13 million people in northern China in 1876–1879: about 5.5 million in Shanxi, 2.5 million in Zhili (now Hebei), 1 million in Henan and 0.5 million in Shandong. Censuses, which include migration from the famine, show a fall of 23 million people, among them 48% of Shanxi’s.

label: Krakatoa erupts in the Sunda Strait
summary: A series of massive explosions on 26–27 August 1883 destroys most of the island of Krakatoa and leaves a caldera in the Sunda Strait. The explosion was heard 3,600 km away in Alice Springs, Australia, and 4,780 km away on Rodrigues near Mauritius. At least 36,417 people died, mostly from the tsunamis that followed.

label: The Berlin Conference and the Scramble for Africa
summary: The Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 regulates European colonisation and trade in Africa and is seen as emblematic of the “Scramble for Africa”, in which Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom claimed most of the continent. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained outside European control.

label: Rinderpest sweeps through the cattle of eastern and southern Africa
summary: A cattle plague present in Abyssinia by 1888 spreads through eastern and southern Africa, reaching South Africa in 1896. The outbreak of the 1890s killed an estimated 80 to 90 percent of all cattle in the two regions. How it entered Africa is debated, and one study finds no evidence that Italian troops brought it with infected oxen from India.

summary: African trypanosomiasis, or sleeping sickness, an infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma brucei and carried by the tsetse fly, has three major outbreaks in recent history, of which the first runs from 1896 to 1906, primarily in Uganda and the Congo Basin. label: The Dunhuang manuscripts are found in the Mogao Caves
summary: In 1900 the itinerant Daoist monk Wang Yuanlu discovers a large and varied collection of religious and secular manuscripts, handwritten on hemp, silk and paper with some woodblock-printed items, in Chinese, Tibetan and other languages, at the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang in Gansu. The documents were produced between the late 4th and early 11th centuries and sealed in the Library Cave (Cave 17); Wang later sold manuscripts to Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot for a modest sum, and some scholars call their removal plunder.
